newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada renews debate on separatist opposition.
newsitem.headline: Canada renews debate on separatist opposition.

text.p: Dissension over the new leader of the Bloc Quebecois is revived debate on Monday over whether the separatist party should remain Canada's official parliamentary opposition.

The weekend election of former communist Gilles Duceppe as leader of the Bloc -- which advocates independence for the French-speaking province of Quebec -- prompted Bloc Member of Parliament Nic LeBlanc to quit the party.

That reduced the Bloc to 50 seats in Canada's elected House of Commons, the same as the right-wing Reform Party. Reform now wants a free vote among opposition members to see who should be the official opposition.

"This is separatists in the House of Commons, who have no use for it, no respect for her majesty, yet they are her majesty's loyal official opposition," said Deborah Grey, Reform caucus chairwoman and deputy parliamentary leader.
Britain's Queen Elizabeth is Canada's head of state.
"What we need to do is get enough opposition independent members to say to the speaker, 'I'm sick of having an official opposition that are separatists'," Grey said in a telephone interview.
"I'd be willing to participate in a free vote of the opposition members on who we want the official opposition to be," she added.
The speaker of the House would need to decide whether to hold such a vote, Grey said.
In February 1996, Reform and the Bloc were in a similar situation, when both parties had 52 seats. But the speaker ruled that the Bloc should remain the official opposition.
The Liberal government of Prime Minister Jean Chretien, which holds a comfortable majority, is expected to call an election this year.
